about.p: A *phrasal verb* is a verb with one or two small words called *particles* – *give up*, *look after*, *put up with*. Together they make a new meaning that you often can't guess from the parts: if you *give up* sugar, you don't 'give' anything anywhere. Phrasal verbs are everywhere in everyday British English – in conversation, emails, television and the news.

Units 1–5 explain how phrasal verbs work: their grammar, their meanings, the particles, the nouns and adjectives formed from them, and register. Units 6–21 look at the commonest verbs (*come*, *get*, *go*, *look*, *make*, *put*, *take*) and particles (*up*, *out*, *off* and the rest). Units 22–70 teach phrasal verbs by concept, by function and by topic – from time and change to work, money, relationships, travel and technology.

about.-: Learn each phrasal verb with its meaning and an example. The notes on the cards tell you when a verb is informal and when its object can go between the verb and the particle (*separable*).
*Complete the phrase* questions hide the particle and ask you to choose it – the part learners most often get wrong.
Work through Units 1–5 first: they make every other unit easier.

units.sub: pick up, turn down, run out of

L.h: A What is a phrasal verb?

L.p: A *phrasal verb* is a verb followed by one or two *particles* – small words such as *up*, *out*, *off*, *in* or *down*. Some phrasal verbs have obvious meanings: if you *pick up* a pen, you lift it from the table. Many others have meanings that are hard to guess: if you *turn down* an offer, you refuse it, and if you *run out of* milk, you have none left.

L.e: Could you pick up that pen for me? She turned down the job because the pay was too low. We've run out of milk again. The plane took off half an hour late. I've given up trying to understand him.

L.h: B With and without an object

L.p: Some phrasal verbs have no object: *The plane took off*, *Please sit down*, *The car broke down*. Others need one: *She picked up the keys*, *I look after my niece on Fridays*. With many of these, the object can go before or after the particle – *turn the radio up* or *turn up the radio*. These are called *separable* phrasal verbs. A pronoun object (*it*, *them*, *her*) always sits in the middle: *turn it up*, never *turn up it*.

L.e: Our car broke down on the motorway. Could you turn the radio up? Could you turn up the radio? Turn it up – I love this song! Who looks after the children while you're at work?

L.x: I love this song – *turn it up* (not *turn up it*)!

L.p: Some phrasal verbs have two particles: *run out of*, *look forward to*, *put up with* (accept something unpleasant), *get on with* (have a good relationship with). With these three-part verbs, the object always comes at the end: *I can't put up with this noise any longer*.

L.e: I'm really looking forward to the holidays. How do you put up with his snoring? Do you get on with your neighbours? We ran out of petrol ten miles from home.

units.sub: take off, give up, find out

L.p: Some phrasal verbs are *literal*: you can work out the meaning from the parts. If you *take off* your coat, you remove it; if you *go out*, you leave the building. Others are *idiomatic*: *take off* can also mean become successful very quickly, and *go out* can mean stop burning. Idiomatic meanings have to be learnt one by one.

L.e: Take off your shoes before you come in. Her online business really took off last year. I'm just going out for a walk. The fire went out during the night. Look up any words you don't know.

L.p: Many common phrasal verbs have several meanings, and the context tells you which one is intended. *Pick up* can mean lift, collect someone, learn without studying, or improve. *Work out* can mean calculate, find the answer to a problem, or do exercise. *Make up* can mean invent a story or excuse, or become friends again after an argument.

L.e: I picked up a few words of Turkish on holiday. Can you pick me up from the station? Business is picking up after a slow winter. Can you work out how much we owe? My brother works out every morning before breakfast. He made up an excuse about his train. They had a row but made up the next day.

L.x: I *picked up* (not *took up*) some Italian while I was working in Rome.

L.h: C Phrasal verbs and one-word verbs

L.p: Many phrasal verbs have a more formal one-word equivalent: *find out* – *discover*, *put off* – *postpone*, *go up* – *increase*, *carry out* – *conduct*. In conversation, phrasal verbs sound more natural; in formal writing, the single word is often better. Compare *We've put off the meeting* with *The meeting has been postponed*.

L.e: When did you find out about the accident? We'll have to put off the party until next week. Prices have gone up again. The tests were carried out in a laboratory.

units.sub: up, out, on, off

L.p: Particles often add a regular meaning. *Up* can mean increase (*speak up*, *turn up*) or completely (*use up*, *eat up*, *tidy up*). *Down* can mean decrease (*slow down*, *cut down*) or on paper (*write down*, *note down*).

L.e: Could you speak up? We can't hear you at the back. Who's used up all the milk? Eat up your vegetables! Slow down – you're driving too fast. Write down your password somewhere safe.

L.p: *Out* can mean not included (*leave out*), aloud (*call out*, *read out*) or until nothing is left (*sell out*, *die out*). *Off* often means leaving (*set off*, *see someone off*) or ending (*call off*, *switch off*).

L.e: Don't leave out any details. The teacher read out the results. The concert sold out in an hour. We set off at dawn. The match was called off because of fog. Switch off the lights when you leave.

L.x: The tickets *sold out* (not *sold off*) in less than an hour.

L.p: *On* often means continue (*carry on*, *go on*, *keep on*). *In* often means entering or including (*join in*, *fill in*, *move in*). Knowing these patterns helps you to guess the meaning of new phrasal verbs, although not every verb follows them.

L.e: Carry on reading until I get back. She kept on asking the same question. The children all joined in the song. Please fill in this form. Our new neighbours moved in last week.

units.sub: breakdown, outcome, run-down

L.p: Many phrasal verbs have related nouns. Some put the verb first: *a breakdown* (from *break down*), *check-in* (*check in*), *a takeover* (*take over*), *a workout* (*work out*). Others put the particle first: *an outcome* (the result), *an outbreak* (*break out*), *an upbringing* (*bring up*). Check the spelling: some are written as one word, some with a hyphen.

L.e: We had a breakdown on the way to the coast. Check-in closes forty minutes before departure. The takeover was announced on Monday. Nobody could predict the outcome of the election. There has been an outbreak of flu at the school. She had a strict upbringing.

L.x: The flu *outbreak* (not *breakout*) closed three schools.

L.p: Some adjectives come from phrasal verbs too: *run-down* (in poor condition), *worn out* (very tired), *built-up* (with many buildings), *well-off* (rich) and *laid-back* (relaxed). Many of them take a hyphen before a noun: *a run-down hotel*, *a built-up area*.

L.e: They bought a run-down cottage and restored it. I feel completely worn out. We live in a built-up area. His family are quite well-off. She has a very laid-back attitude to deadlines.

L.p: Nouns from phrasal verbs are very common in news and business English: *cutbacks* in spending, a *setback* for the team, a high *turnout*, a *crackdown* on crime. They let you say a lot in a few words: *a breakdown in talks* instead of *the talks broke down*.

L.e: Cutbacks in funding have closed the library. The injury was a setback for the team. Turnout at the election was low. Police have announced a crackdown on speeding.

units.sub: dig up, pore over, chill out

L.p: Many phrasal verbs use a physical action as a *metaphor* for something abstract. Journalists *dig up* information (find hidden facts, as if digging in the ground); jobs *pile up* (increase, like objects in a heap); tension *boils over* (becomes angry and uncontrolled, like a pan of milk). One person's mood can *rub off on* others. Seeing the picture behind the verb helps you to remember it.

L.e: The reporter dug up some embarrassing facts about the minister. Work has really piled up while I've been away. Tension between the neighbours finally boiled over. Her enthusiasm rubbed off on the whole class.

L.p: Some phrasal verbs are formal. You *pore over* documents (study them carefully), *embark on* a project (start it), *adhere to* rules (follow them), *dispose of* waste (get rid of it) and *account for* something (explain it, or form a part of it). These are common in reports and official writing.

L.e: Lawyers pored over the contract for days. The university is embarking on a major building programme. All staff must adhere to the safety guidelines. Please dispose of used batteries carefully. Tourism accounts for a third of the island's income.

L.x: All staff must *adhere to* (not *adhere with*) the guidelines.

L.p: Many phrasal verbs are informal and best kept for conversation and messages: *chill out* (relax), *hang out* (spend time somewhere with friends), *mess about* (behave in a silly way), *pig out* (eat a lot), *throw up* (be sick) and *suss out* (understand, British English). Use them with friends, but not in an essay or a job application.

L.e: I'm just going to chill out this weekend. We used to hang out at the park after school. Stop messing about and help me! We pigged out on pizza last night. I couldn't suss out what he wanted.

units.sub: come across, come up with, come round

L.p: You *come across* something when you find it by chance, and you *come up with* an idea or plan when you think of it. A subject *comes up* when someone mentions it, and a problem *comes up* when it happens unexpectedly. The truth *comes out* when it becomes known, and a book or film *comes out* when it is published or released.

L.e: I came across some old letters in the attic. She came up with a brilliant idea for the party. Your name came up at the meeting. Something's come up – I can't make it tonight. The truth eventually came out. Her new album comes out next month.

L.x: She *came up with* (not *came up*) a great solution.

L.h: B Visiting and changing your mind

L.p: You *come round* (or *come over*) when you visit someone's home. *Come round to* something means change your opinion and agree with it. You *come back* when you return, and you *come along* when you go somewhere with someone.

L.e: Why don't you come round for dinner on Friday? Dad didn't like the idea at first, but he's come round to it. When are you coming back from Spain? We're going to the beach – do you want to come along?

L.p: If you *come through* a difficult experience, you survive it. You *come down with* an illness when you start to have it. A plan *comes off* when it succeeds (informal), and a bill *comes to* a total. When you ask how something *came about*, you want to know how it happened.

L.e: She came through the operation well. My throat is sore – I must be coming down with something. The surprise party didn't come off – she found out. The bill came to over £200. How did the misunderstanding come about?

units.sub: get over, get by, get away with

L.p: You *get over* an illness or a disappointment when you recover from it. You *get by* when you manage, but only just – with little money or limited skills. You *get through* a difficult time (survive it) or a pile of work (finish it). If you *get round* a problem, you find a way to avoid it.

L.e: My cousin never really got over losing his dog. We get by on one salary. I can get by in French, but I'm not fluent. I don't know how I got through that first winter. We got round the parking problem by taking the train.

L.p: If you *get away with* something wrong, you are not punished for it. You *get out of* a duty when you avoid doing it, and you *get away* when you escape or go on holiday. Informally, you *get at* someone when you keep criticising them, and you *get back at* someone when you take revenge.

L.e: He cheated in the test and got away with it. I'm trying to get out of the meeting tomorrow. The thieves got away in a stolen car. We're hoping to get away for a few days in May. Why are you always getting at me? She got back at him by telling everyone his secret.

L.x: He *got away with* (not *got away from*) cheating in the exam.

L.p: You *get along with* people when you have a friendly relationship. You *get on* in life or at work when you make progress. You *get across* an idea when you make people understand it, and you *get down to* work when you start it seriously. Something that *gets you down* makes you feel sad.

L.e: I get along really well with my sister-in-law. She's very ambitious and wants to get on. It's hard to get across such a complicated idea. Let's get down to business. This grey weather is getting me down.

units.sub: go off, go through, go along with

L.p: Food *goes off* when it becomes bad (British English); an alarm or a bomb *goes off* when it rings or explodes; and you *go off* someone or something when you stop liking them. Things *go on* (happen or continue), prices go up or *go down*, and in the evening you *go out* with friends.

L.e: This milk has gone off – smell it. The fire alarm went off at three in the morning. I went off coffee when I was ill. What's going on in there? The meeting went on for hours. Petrol prices have gone down a little.

L.p: You *go through* a difficult experience when you suffer it, and you *go through* a document when you examine it carefully. You *go over* something when you check or repeat it. You *go without* something you can't have, and you *go for* something when you choose it or try hard to get it.

L.e: She went through a terrible time after the accident. Let's go through the contract together. Can we go over the main points once more? We had to go without heating for a week. I'll go for the fish, please. If you want the job, go for it!

L.x: Let's *go over* (not *go above*) the answers before the test.

L.p: If you *go along with* a plan or a person, you agree, often without enthusiasm. Colours or clothes that *go with* each other look good together. You *go back on* a promise when you don't keep it, and an event *goes ahead* when it takes place as planned.

L.e: I didn't like the idea, but I went along with it. Does this tie go with my shirt? The government went back on its promise to cut taxes. 'Can I use your phone?' 'Go ahead.' The concert will go ahead despite the rain.

units.sub: look into, look up to, look forward to

L.p: You *look for* something you have lost or want to find, and you *look into* a problem when you investigate it. You *look up* a word in a dictionary or a fact online, and you *look through* papers when you read them quickly. When you *look over* a document, you check it.

L.e: I've been looking for my glasses all morning. The police are looking into the complaint. Look up the train times before we leave. I looked through the brochures but found nothing I liked. Could you look over my essay before I hand it in?

L.x: The police are *looking into* (not *looking in*) the complaint.

L.p: If you *look up to* someone, you admire and respect them; if you *look down on* someone, you think you are better than them. You look after someone when you take care of them, and you *look out for* someone when you protect them.

L.e: I've always looked up to my older sister. Some people look down on anyone without a degree. Who will look after the cat while we're away? Big brothers should look out for their younger siblings.

L.h: C The future, the past and warnings

L.p: You *look forward to* something pleasant in the future. *Look out!* is a warning of danger. You *look ahead* when you think about the future, and you *look back on* the past. A situation *is looking up* when it is improving.

L.e: I'm looking forward to meeting your parents. Look out! There's a car coming! We need to look ahead and plan for next year. When I look back on my school days, I remember the friends most. Things are looking up – I've got an interview.

units.sub: make up, make out, make for

L.p: *Make up* has several meanings. You *make up* a story or an excuse when you invent it. People *make it up* after an argument when they become friends again. Parts *make up* a whole when they form it. You *make up for* something bad by doing something good, and you *make up your mind* when you decide.

L.e: She made up a story about a dragon for the children. They argued all evening but made it up before bed. Women make up over half of the workforce. I bought her flowers to make up for being late. I can't make up my mind about the job offer.

L.x: Women *make up* (not *make out*) over half the staff.

L.p: You *make out* something when you manage to see, hear or read it with difficulty. You make out a cheque when you write it. You can't make someone out when you can't understand their character, and you *make out that* something is true when you claim it, often falsely.

L.e: I could just make out a figure in the fog. Can you make out what he's saying? Who should I make the cheque out to? I can't make him out – one day he's friendly, the next he ignores me. She made out that she'd never met him, but she had.

L.h: C Other phrasal verbs with make

L.p: You *make for* a place when you go towards it, and things *make for* a particular result when they help to create it. A thief *makes off with* the things he steals. *Make do with* means accept something less good because there is nothing better.

L.e: As soon as the rain started, we made for the nearest café. Good weather makes for a pleasant holiday. The thief made off with my handbag. There was no milk, so we made do with black tea.

units.sub: put off, put up with, put across

L.p: You *put off* an event when you delay it, and you put off doing something when you avoid starting it. Something *puts you off* when it makes you not want to do or have it. You *put aside* money when you save it, and you *put back* an event when you move it to a later time.

L.e: The match has been put off until next week. I keep putting off going to the dentist. The smell put me off my food. I put aside some money every month. The meeting has been put back to Thursday.

L.x: The bad reviews *put me off* (not *put me down*) going to see the film.

L.p: You *put up with* something unpleasant when you accept it without complaining. You *put someone up* when you let them stay at your home. People also *put up* buildings, tents and notices, and landlords *put up the rent* when they raise it.

L.e: Her flatmate plays drums at midnight, and somehow she puts up with it. Can you put me up for a night when I'm in Leeds? They're putting up a new hotel opposite the station. The landlord has put up the rent again.

L.p: You *put across* an idea when you explain it clearly, and you *put forward* a plan when you offer it for discussion. You *put someone down* when you make them feel stupid. Firefighters *put out* a fire when they stop it burning.

L.e: She's good at putting across complicated ideas. The committee put forward three proposals. Her boss is always putting her down in meetings. Firefighters took two hours to put out the blaze.

units.sub: take after, take up, take in

L.p: You *take after* a parent or relative when you look or behave like them. You *take to* someone when you start to like them, and you *take someone out* when you take them to a restaurant or the cinema and pay. You *take back* something you said when you admit it was wrong.

L.e: She takes after her grandmother – they're both stubborn. The children took to their new teacher immediately. He took me out for dinner on my birthday. Sorry – I was wrong, and I take back that remark.

L.x: She *takes after* (not *takes from*) her father.

L.p: You *take up* a hobby or sport when you start it, and things *take up* time or space when they fill it. A company *takes on* staff when it employs them, and you take on work when you accept it. One company *takes over* another when it gains control of it.

L.e: I took up yoga last year. This sofa takes up half the room. The factory is taking on fifty new workers. I've taken on too much work this month. The bank was taken over by a German group.

L.p: You *take in* information when you understand and remember it, but you *are taken in* when someone deceives you. You *take off* a person when you copy their voice or manner to make people laugh. You *take down* details when you write them, and you *take apart* a machine when you separate it into pieces.

L.e: There was too much information to take in. Don't be taken in by his charm. She takes off our teacher brilliantly. The police officer took down my details. He took the clock apart to see how it worked.

units.sub: speak up, use up, do up

L.p: *Up* often shows an increase or an upward movement. Prices *go up*, you turn up the heating, you *speak up* when people can't hear you, and business *picks up* when it improves. You *bring up* a subject when you mention it, and you *bring up* children when you raise them.

L.e: Turn up the heating – it's freezing. Speak up, please – the line's bad. Trade usually picks up in the spring. I didn't want to bring up the subject of money. She was brought up by her aunt in Glasgow.

L.x: She was *brought up* (not *grown up*) by her grandparents.

L.p: *Up* can also mean completely or until nothing is left. You *use up* the paper, eat up your dinner and *drink up* your tea. You *do up* a coat when you fasten it, and an old house when you repair and decorate it. You *fill up* the car with petrol.

L.e: Who used up all the hot water? Drink up – we're leaving. Do up your coat; it's cold outside. They're doing up an old farmhouse in Wales. Let's fill up the tank before the motorway.

L.p: *Up* can also suggest appearing. Someone *turns up* when they arrive, often unexpectedly, and problems *crop up*. You *keep up* when you stay at the same speed or level as others. You *own up* when you admit you did something wrong.

L.e: He turned up an hour late without apologising. A few problems have cropped up with the new software. Walk faster – I can't keep up! In the end, the boy owned up to breaking the window.

units.sub: find out, sort out, stand out

L.p: *Out* often suggests discovering or solving. You *find out* information, *work out* an answer, *figure out* how something works (informal) and *sort out* a problem or a mess. You *check out* a place when you go and see whether it is good.

L.e: I found out yesterday that I'd passed. Can you work out how long the journey will take? I can't figure out how to switch this thing on. The bank has finally sorted out the mistake on my account. Let's check out that new café on the corner.

L.x: I'll *sort out* (not *sort up*) the problem tomorrow.

L.p: *Out* can mean removing or excluding. You *leave out* information (don't include it), *cross out* a mistake (draw a line through it), *rule out* a possibility (decide it can't be true) and *drop out* of a course (leave before the end). A custom or a species *dies out* when it disappears completely.

L.e: You've left out the most important part. Cross out any wrong answers neatly. Police have ruled out murder. He dropped out of university after a year. Many local languages are dying out.

L.p: *Out* can also mean becoming visible or noticeable. Something *stands out* when it is easy to notice or better than others. The sun *comes out*, and so do flowers when they open. You *call out* when you shout, and you *point out* something when you make others notice it.

L.e: Her bright red coat stood out in the crowd. The sun came out just as we reached the beach. Someone in the audience called out my name. She pointed out a mistake in my calculations.

units.sub: set off, call off, put off

L.p: *Off* often describes leaving. You *set off* on a journey, a plane *takes off*, and you *see someone off* when you go to the station or airport to say goodbye. Informally, someone who *nods off* falls asleep for a short time.

L.e: We set off for the coast at six in the morning. The plane took off twenty minutes late. My parents came to the airport to see me off. Halfway through the sermon, an old man in the front row nodded off.

L.x: We *set off* (not *set up*) on our journey at dawn.

L.p: *Off* can mean ending or removing. You *call off* an event (cancel it), *switch off* a machine and *break off* a relationship or talks (end them suddenly). Pain or a drug *wears off* when its effect gradually disappears. A company *lays off* workers when it stops employing them.

L.e: They called off the wedding a week before the date. Don't forget to switch off the oven. The two countries have broken off talks. The painkillers are starting to wear off. The factory laid off two hundred workers.

L.h: C Off = success, noise and other meanings

L.p: You *pull off* something difficult when you manage to do it. A bomb or an alarm *goes off* when it explodes or rings. Something *puts you off* when it makes you dislike it. You *show off* when you try to impress people, and you are *cut off* when a phone call ends suddenly.

L.e: Nobody thought he could win, but he pulled it off. A car alarm went off outside my window. The long queue put me off. He's always showing off about his new car. I was talking to my sister in Canada when suddenly we got cut off.

units.sub: carry on, hand in, join in

L.p: *On* often means continuing. You *carry on* doing something, *keep on* doing something (often annoyingly) and *move on* to the next topic. You *hold on* when you wait, especially on the phone. A meeting *drags on* when it lasts too long.

L.e: Carry on with your work while I make a call. He kept on interrupting me. Let's move on to the next item on the agenda. Hold on – I'll just get a pen. The meeting dragged on until seven.

L.p: *On* can describe wearing or connecting. You *put on* clothes, and you *try on* clothes in a shop to see if they fit. You *switch on* a light or machine. Informally, you *catch on* when you start to understand, and an idea *catches on* when it becomes popular.

L.e: Put on a jumper if you're cold. Can I try on these jeans? Switch on the light, please. Everyone else laughed, but I didn't catch on until later.

L.x: *Put on* (not *dress*) your coat before you go out.

L.p: *In* often suggests entering or including. You *check in* at a hotel or airport and *drop in* on a friend (visit without arranging it). You *join in* an activity and *hand in* homework or a document (give it to a teacher or official). You *give in* when you stop resisting.

L.e: We checked in at the hotel at about nine. Drop in for a cup of tea any time. Everyone joined in the singing. Please hand in your essays by Friday. The children kept asking until their mother gave in.

units.sub: turn down, slow down, think over

L.h: A Down = less, lower or defeated

L.p: *Down* often means reducing or becoming less. You *calm down*, slow down and *cut down on* sugar. Someone *backs down* when they stop arguing or demanding. You *turn down* an offer when you refuse it, and you *let someone down* when you disappoint them.

L.e: Calm down – it's only a scratch. My doctor says I should cut down on salt and fried food. The union refused to back down. She turned down a place at Cambridge. I promised to help, and I won't let you down.

L.x: I promised to help, so I won't *let you down* (not *let you off*).

L.h: B Down = writing, stopping or failing

L.p: *Down* is used for writing: you write down, *note down* or take down information. It can also mean stopping or failing: a car or talks *break down*, a business *closes down*, and a computer system goes down. A leader *steps down* when they leave an important job.

L.e: Note down the main points as you listen. Talks broke down after only an hour. The shop on the corner has closed down. The website went down for three hours. The chairman is stepping down at the end of the year.

L.h: C Over = thinking, checking or passing

L.p: *Over* often suggests careful thought or checking. You *think over* an offer, *talk over* a problem and *go over* your notes. *Over* can also mean a change of control: you *hand over* the keys or responsibility to someone. An argument or storm *blows over* when it passes without serious effect.

L.e: Think it over and let me know tomorrow. We talked over the problem for hours. Go over your answers before you hand them in. At midnight the night nurse handed over to the day team. Don't worry – the argument will soon blow over.

units.sub: come about, mess around, bring about

L.h: A Around and about = without a purpose

L.p: *Around* and *about* (often interchangeable in British English) can mean without a clear purpose. You *hang around* (wait or spend time doing nothing in particular), *wander around* a town and *mess around* (behave in a silly way). In British English, people *potter about* when they do small jobs in a relaxed way.

L.e: Teenagers were hanging around outside the shop. We spent the afternoon wandering around the old town. Stop messing around and do your homework! On Sundays my dad likes to potter about in the garden.

L.h: B Around = turning, visiting and spreading

L.p: These particles also describe movement in different directions. You *turn around* (face the other way), *look around* a place (visit it) and *show someone around*. News *gets around* when it spreads, and you *shop around* when you compare prices in several shops.

L.e: She turned around and walked out. Would you like to look around the house? Our guide showed us around the castle. News of the engagement soon got around. Shop around before you buy a new phone.

L.h: C Bring about, come about, go about

L.p: *Bring about* means cause something to happen, especially a change, and *come about* means happen. You *go about* a task when you start dealing with it in a particular way, and you *set about* something when you begin it with energy. You *bring someone round* when you persuade them to agree.

L.e: The internet has brought about huge changes in how we shop. How did this situation come about? How should I go about finding a flat? She set about cleaning the kitchen. At first he hated the plan, but we brought him round.

L.x: The war *brought about* (not *brought up*) enormous changes.

units.sub: stand for, deal with, part with

L.p: You *ask for* something you want. You *fall for* a trick when you believe it, and you fall for a person when you fall in love. Letters *stand for* words (*BBC* stands for *British Broadcasting Corporation*), and a party or person stands for a principle when they support it. You *account for* a fact when you explain it.

L.e: I asked for the bill. I can't believe you fell for that old trick! He fell for her the moment they met. What does UN stand for? The party stands for equality and fairness. How do you account for the missing money?

L.x: What does EU *stand for* (not *mean for*)?

L.p: You *deal with* a problem or a person when you take action or handle them. You *cope with* difficulty (manage it) and put up with annoyance (accept it). You *part with* something when you give it away, often unwillingly, and you *do without* something you can't have.

L.e: Who deals with complaints in this company? She's coping well with three small children. I hate parting with old books. We'll have to do without a car for a while.

L.h: C More verbs with fixed prepositions

L.p: Some verbs are always followed by the same preposition: *care for* (look after), *call for* (demand or need), *head for* (go towards), *side with* (support in an argument) and *tamper with* (change something without permission, to damage it).

L.e: She cared for her mother for ten years. The situation calls for urgent action. At the end of the day, we headed for home. My parents always sided with my brother. Someone had tampered with the brakes.

units.sub: go through, cut back, get back

L.p: *Through* often means from beginning to end. You *go through* a hard time, *get through* an exam or a pile of work, *read through* a document and *see* something *through* (continue until it is finished). A plan *falls through* when it fails to happen. On the phone, you get through when you are connected.

L.e: They went through a difficult few years after the factory closed. I don't know how I got through all that marking. Read through your essay before you hand it in. It was hard, but she saw the project through. Our holiday plans fell through at the last minute.

L.x: Our plans *fell through* (not *fell down*) at the last minute.

L.p: *Back* usually means returning. You *get back* home, *give back* something you borrowed, *call back* (phone again) and *pay back* money you owe. You *get back to* someone when you reply to them later.

L.e: What time did you get back last night? Can you give me back my pen? I'll call you back in five minutes. I'll pay you back on Friday. Let me check and get back to you.

L.h: C Back = reduce, retreat or support

L.p: *Back* can also mean reducing or retreating. Companies *cut back* when they spend less, and you *hold back* when you don't show your feelings. You *back out* of an agreement when you decide not to do what you promised, and you *back someone up* when you support them.

L.e: We've had to cut back on staff this year. She held back her tears. They backed out of the deal at the last minute. If they question it, I'll back you up.

units.sub: run into, look into, give away

L.h: A Into = meeting, entering or changing

L.p: *Into* often suggests entering or meeting. You *bump into* someone when you meet them by chance, and a plan *runs into* problems when it starts to have them. Thieves *break into* a building (enter it illegally), and you *talk someone into* something when you persuade them. One thing *turns into* another when it changes.

L.e: I bumped into my old teacher at the supermarket. The project ran into problems in its first month. Thieves broke into the shop overnight. She talked me into buying a new bike. The caterpillar turned into a beautiful butterfly.

L.x: I *bumped into* (not *bumped with*) an old friend in town.

L.p: *Away* often means leaving or removing. You *go away* on holiday and *run away* from danger. You *put away* things (put them in their usual place), *throw away* rubbish and *give away* things you don't want – or a secret, by mistake. A sound or feeling *fades away* when it gradually disappears.

L.e: We're going away for the weekend. The boy ran away from home at fifteen. Put your toys away before dinner. Don't throw away those boxes – we can use them. I gave away all my old books. The music faded away into silence.

L.p: *Away* can also mean doing something continuously: you *work away* at a task and *chat away* to a friend. Time *slips away* when it passes quickly. If you *do away with* something, you get rid of it completely.

L.e: He was working away at his computer all evening. The two old friends chatted away for hours. The days slipped away and the holiday was over. The school has done away with uniforms.

units.sub: while away, hang around, laze about

L.p: You *while away* hours when you spend them pleasantly while waiting. On holiday you *laze about* (relax and do nothing) or *lounge about* (sit or lie in a relaxed way). You *hang around* somewhere when you wait there. Someone who wastes time or money on unimportant things *fritters it away*.

L.e: We whiled away the afternoon playing cards. I spent the weekend lazing about at home. The students lounged about on the grass. We hung around for an hour, but she didn't come. He frittered away his savings on gadgets.

L.p: You *set aside* time for an activity when you keep it free for that purpose, and you *fit in* an activity when you find time for it. You *catch up on* sleep or work you have missed, and you finally *get round to* something you have been meaning to do. When you have a holiday from work, you *take time off*.

L.e: I set aside an hour every evening for reading. Can you fit in a meeting on Thursday? I'll catch up on my emails this weekend. I never got round to fixing the shelf. She's taking time off in June.

L.x: I finally *got round to* (not *got around for*) painting the kitchen.

L.p: At the end of the day you *turn in* (go to bed, informal) or *stay up* late. You might *doze off* – fall asleep without meaning to – in front of the television. At the weekend you can *lie in* (British English), staying in bed later than usual.

L.e: I'm exhausted – I think I'll turn in. We stayed up until two talking. Dad always dozes off during the news. On Sundays I like to lie in until ten.

units.sub: drag on, wear off, catch up

L.p: Time *goes by* (passes). A boring period *drags on*, but a happy one *flies by*. An event that happens regularly *comes round* again, and as an evening *wears on* it gets later and later.

L.e: As the years went by, they saw less of each other. The summer flew by. The negotiations dragged on into the night. Before we knew it, exam time had come round again. As the evening wore on, the guests began to leave.

L.p: Traffic or problems can *hold you up* (delay you). Appointments *run late* when they happen later than planned, and a meeting *runs over* when it lasts longer than planned. You *fall behind* with work or payments when you don't do enough, *catch up with* others when you reach their level, and *keep up with* changes when you stay at the same level.

L.e: Sorry I'm late – I was held up at the station. The doctor's appointments are running late today. The meeting ran over by half an hour. I fell behind with my studies when I was ill. Walk on – I'll catch up with you. It's hard to keep up with all the changes in technology.

L.x: Sorry I'm late – I was *held up* (not *held on*) in traffic.

L.p: Time *runs out* when there is none left. The effect of a drug or a feeling *wears off* when it gradually disappears. An event *winds down* when it gradually comes to an end, and people wind down when they relax after work. Something that *dates back to* a past time started then.

L.e: Time is running out to book your place. The excitement wore off after a few days. The party was winding down by midnight. I like to wind down with a book before bed. The castle dates back to the twelfth century.

units.sub: settle down, move in, stay over

L.p: You *move in* to a new home and *move out* of the old one. You *settle in* when you start to feel comfortable in a new place, and you *settle down* when you start a quiet life in one place, often with a partner. People *move away* from an area when they go to live somewhere else.

L.e: We moved in on a rainy Saturday. The previous tenants moved out a week ago. After years of travelling, he wants to settle down. Most of my friends moved away after school.

L.x: The children soon *settled in* (not *settled on*) at their new school.

L.p: You *stay in* when you remain at home for the evening. You *stay over* at someone's house when you spend the night there, and you *stay on* when you remain longer than planned. You *stop off* somewhere when you visit it during a journey.

L.e: Let's stay in tonight and watch a film. It's late – why don't you stay over? She stayed on at university to do a master's degree. We stopped off in Paris on the way to Rome.

L.p: A house *backs onto* something when it has it behind, and a room *looks out over* a view. A place *tucked away* somewhere is hidden or quiet. A village is *cut off* when snow or floods stop people reaching it, and a car is *boxed in* when other vehicles stop it from moving.

L.e: Our garden backs onto a small park. The bedroom looks out over the harbour. The restaurant is tucked away down a side street. The village was cut off by snow for three days. I couldn't leave – a van had boxed me in.

units.sub: bring about, lead to, stem from

L.p: Several phrasal verbs mean *cause*. *Bring about* is used for changes; *lead to* and *result in* show that one thing causes another. Something can *set off* a reaction or *spark off* a protest or an argument (make it start suddenly). People and newspapers *stir up* trouble or strong feelings, often deliberately.

L.e: The new manager brought about a lot of changes. Lack of sleep can lead to poor concentration. The fire resulted in the closure of the theatre. One careless remark set off a huge row. The arrest sparked off protests across the city. Some newspapers like to stir up trouble.

L.p: Things can *bring on* an illness or a feeling (cause it to start), and dust or noise can *trigger off* a sudden reaction. A song or a smell can *bring back* memories. Something that *cheers you up* makes you happier.

L.e: Cold weather often brings on his asthma. Pollen can trigger off a sneezing fit. That song brings back memories of my first holiday. A phone call from my sister cheered me up.

L.x: Stress can *bring on* (not *bring about*) a migraine.

L.p: To show where something comes from, you can say it *stems from* or *arises from* a cause (formal). When one thing matters more than anything else, everything *comes down to* it. Effects can *spill over* into other areas when they spread.

L.e: Many of her fears stem from her childhood. Problems often arise from poor communication. In the end, it comes down to money. The conflict has spilled over into neighbouring countries.

units.O: Write about a change in your town or country. Explain what brought it about and what it has led to. Use at least eight phrasal verbs from this unit.

units.sub: do up, turn into, switch over

L.p: You *do up* a house when you repair and decorate it, and you *touch up* paint or a photo when you improve small parts of it. You *tone down* language or a design when you make it less strong, and you *step up* efforts or security when you increase them. A tailor can *take in* a dress (make it narrower) or let out trousers (make them wider).

L.e: They're doing up an old cottage in Cornwall. I'll touch up the paint on the door. The advert was toned down after complaints. Police have stepped up security at the airport. The dress was too loose, so I had it taken in.

L.p: One thing *turns into* another when it becomes something different. Children *grow into* clothes (become big enough for them) and *grow out of* them, and they also grow out of habits as they get older. Something that *grows on* you is something you gradually start to like.

L.e: The small village has turned into a busy town. The jacket's a bit big, but he'll grow into it. Most children grow out of their fear of the dark. The music grew on me after a few listens.

L.x: The fishing village has *turned into* (not *turned to*) a busy resort.

L.p: You *switch over* from one system, supplier or TV channel to another. You *swap over* when you exchange places or jobs with someone (informal), and you *change round* the furniture when you move it into new positions. Someone who *comes round* changes their mind and agrees.

L.e: We've switched over to a new energy supplier. Shall we swap over and you drive for a while? We changed the furniture round in the living room. He didn't like the plan at first, but he's come round.

units.sub: pull off, fall through, get ahead

L.p: You *pull off* something difficult when you manage to do it, and a plan *comes off* when it succeeds (informal). Ambitious people want to *get ahead* in their careers. Informally, you *make it* when you finally succeed. Hard work *pays off* when the result makes the effort worthwhile.

L.e: Nobody expected them to pull off the deal. Our plan to surprise her came off perfectly. She'll do anything to get ahead. After years of small parts, he finally made it as an actor. All those hours of practice paid off.

L.x: He *pulled off* (not *pulled out*) an amazing victory.

L.p: A plan *falls through* when it doesn't happen, and a joke or an idea *falls flat* when it fails to have the effect you hoped for. A business *goes under* when it fails and closes. You *let someone down* when you fail to do what they expected, and you *miss out* when you lose a chance.

L.e: The sale of the house fell through. His joke fell flat – nobody laughed. Hundreds of small shops went under during the recession. I'm sorry I let you down. Book now so you don't miss out.

L.p: You *have a go at* something when you try it (informal), and you *go for* something when you try hard to get it. You *keep at* a task when you continue trying, and you *stick at* it when you continue even though it is difficult. Runners *drop out* of a race when they stop before the end.

L.e: I've never surfed before, but I'll have a go at it. If you really want the job, go for it! Keep at it – you're nearly there. Learning the violin is hard, but she stuck at it. Two runners dropped out after ten miles.

units.sub: set up, kick off, wind up

L.p: You *set up* a business or organisation (start it), *start out* in a career and *start off* a meeting or meal with something. A football match *kicks off* when it starts, and informally an event kicks off too. An engine *starts up* when it begins working.

L.e: She set up her own company at twenty-five. He started out as a waiter and now owns three restaurants. Let's start off with a quick introduction. The match kicks off at three. The festival kicks off on Friday with a parade. The engine wouldn't start up in the cold.

L.x: She *set up* (not *set off*) her own company at twenty-five.

L.p: You *finish off* a task or food (complete it), and a chairperson *winds up* a meeting (ends it). You *round off* an evening with something pleasant, and informally you *wrap up* a discussion or a deal when you finish it. A shop or cinema *closes down* when it stops operating for good.

L.e: Let me just finish off this email. The chairman wound up the meeting at five. We rounded off the evening with a walk along the river. Let's wrap up this discussion and go home. The old cinema closed down last year.

L.p: Informally, you *pack in* a job or activity when you stop doing it, and you *knock off* when you stop work for the day. Governments *phase out* things gradually (stop using them step by step). Noise *dies down*, and you *pull out* of an agreement or a race when you withdraw.

L.e: She packed in her job to travel round the world. On Fridays the builders knock off at lunchtime. The government is phasing out petrol cars. The applause finally died down. Two teams pulled out of the competition.

units.sub: pull up, step back, turn round

L.p: You *sit up* (sit with a straight back), lie down and *bend down* to reach something low. You *turn round* to face the other way and *step back* to move away from something. When you lose your balance, you *fall over*; when a car or a person hits you to the ground, you are *knocked over*.

L.e: Sit up straight at the table. He bent down to tie his shoelace. She turned round when I called her name. Step back from the edge of the platform. I slipped on the ice and fell over. A cyclist was knocked over by a bus.

L.x: A cyclist was *knocked over* (not *knocked out*) by a car, but she wasn't badly hurt.

L.p: A car *pulls up* when it comes to a stop somewhere, and a driver *pulls over* when a police officer or a problem makes them stop by the kerb. A train *pulls in* when it arrives at a platform. You *turn off* a main road onto a smaller one. A vehicle that hits a person or animal and drives over them *runs* them *over*.

L.e: A taxi pulled up outside the hotel. Our train pulled in at platform four, ten minutes early. The police told him to pull over. Turn off at the next exit. Sadly, the fox had been run over.

L.p: You *hand out* papers when you give one to each person, *hold up* your hand to answer a question and *hang up* your coat on a hook. After a meal you *clear away* the plates, and in an exam you *turn over* the paper when you are told to start.

L.e: The teacher handed out the exam papers. Hold up your hand if you know the answer. Hang your coat up on the hook. Can you clear away the plates? Turn over the page and begin.

units.sub: blow up, knock down, clear up

L.p: A bomb *blows up* a building or a bridge (destroys it). Old buildings are *knocked down* or *pulled down* (demolished). A house *burns down* when fire destroys it. Floods *wash away* roads, and strong winds *blow down* trees and power lines.

L.e: The old factory was knocked down to make way for flats. Rebels blew up the railway bridge. The barn burned down in the night. The flood washed away part of the road. Hundreds of trees were blown down in the storm.

L.x: The old cinema was *knocked down* (not *knocked out*) to make room for flats.

L.p: A ship *breaks up* on rocks (separates into pieces), and old shoes *fall apart*. You *tear up* paper when you tear it into small pieces, and vandals *smash up* things when they break them violently. A car is *written off* when it is too badly damaged to repair.

L.e: The ship broke up on the rocks. My old trainers are falling apart. She tore up his letter without reading it. Vandals smashed up the bus shelter. The car was written off after the accident.

L.p: After a disaster, people *clear up* the mess, *sweep up* broken glass and *mop up* water. Rescue workers *dig out* survivors trapped under buildings. Insurance companies *pay out* for the damage, and families slowly *pick up the pieces* – return to normal life.

L.e: It took weeks to clear up after the floods. Sweep up the broken glass carefully. We mopped up the water with old towels. Rescuers dug out three survivors. The insurance company paid out for the damage. After the fire, the family slowly picked up the pieces.

units.O: Write a short news report about a storm, flood or fire and how people recovered. Use at least eight phrasal verbs from this unit.

units.sub: speak up, point out, sum up

L.p: You *speak up* when you speak more loudly, and you *speak out* when you criticise something publicly. You *point out* a fact (draw attention to it), *bring up* a subject (mention it) and *sum up* (give a short summary). When you *spell out* something, you explain it very clearly and in detail.

L.e: Could you speak up a bit? Several doctors have spoken out against the plan. She pointed out a mistake in the figures. I didn't want to bring up the subject of money. To sum up, the project was a success. Let me spell out exactly what I expect from you.

L.x: She *pointed out* (not *showed out*) a mistake in my essay.

L.p: Informally, you *butt in* when you interrupt rudely, you *chip in* when you add a comment, and you *go on* when you talk about something for too long. You *come across* well or badly when you make a good or bad impression. A conversation *dries up* when people run out of things to say.

L.e: Sorry to butt in, but there's a phone call for you. Everyone chipped in with ideas. He went on about his holiday for an hour. She comes across as very confident. After the first ten minutes, the conversation dried up.

L.p: You *jot down* information (write it quickly), *fill in* a form and *send off* an application. When you can't answer at once, you *get back to* someone later. Informally, you *drop someone a line* when you write them a short message.

L.e: Jot down your ideas as they come to you. Please fill in both sides of the form. I sent off my application yesterday. I'll get back to you by Friday. Drop me a line when you arrive.

units.sub: stand out, take after, look up to

L.p: You *take after* a parent when you look or behave like them. Some people *stand out* in a crowd – they are easy to notice, or better than others. You *look up to* someone you admire. A person can *come across* as rude or friendly, and a shy person may *open up* (start to talk about their feelings) once they trust you.

L.e: Jack takes after his father – they have the same laugh. With her bright orange hair, she always stands out. I've always looked up to my older brother. He comes across as rude, but he's just shy. After a few weeks, she began to open up.

L.p: You *show off* when you try to impress people, and you *put it on* when you pretend to have a feeling. Someone *lives up to* their reputation when they are as good as people expect. A loyal friend *sticks up for* you when others criticise you (informal).

L.e: Stop showing off – nobody's impressed. He's not really upset; he's putting it on. The new manager has lived up to her reputation. My sister always stuck up for me at school.

L.x: The film *lived up to* (not *lived to*) all our expectations.

L.p: A town *spreads out* along a river or coast, and a narrow path *opens out* into a wider space. A quiet place *livens up* when it becomes busier and more exciting. An area that is *run-down* is in poor condition.

L.e: The village spreads out along the valley. The narrow street opens out into a pretty square. The resort really livens up in August. The town centre is quite run-down now.

units.sub: turn out, break out, go off

L.p: Events *take place* (happen as planned), *go ahead* (happen despite doubts) or are *put off* (delayed). War, fire and fighting *break out* (start suddenly). An event *goes off* well or badly – it is successful or not – and a protest or celebration can *spill over* into the streets.

L.e: The wedding took place in a small chapel. The concert will go ahead despite the rain. Fighting broke out between rival fans. The fireworks display went off without a hitch. The celebrations spilled over into the early hours.

L.x: War *broke out* (not *broke up*) in 1914.

L.p: People *turn out* for an event when they go to it, and the number who come is the *turnout*. Crowds *pour in* (arrive in large numbers), *gather round* to watch and *spill out* of a stadium at the end. The police *hold back* a crowd when they stop it moving forward, and people *push in* when they join a queue in front of others.

L.e: Thousands turned out to welcome the team home. Fans poured in through the gates. People gathered round to watch the street performer. The crowd spilled out onto the streets after the match. Police struggled to hold back the crowds. Hey – don't push in!

L.p: Something *turns out* well or badly – it has a good or bad result – and a fact *turns out* to be true when you discover it is true. Excitement *dies down* when it becomes less, and a scandal *blows over* when people forget it. Organisers *lay on* food or transport for a big event.

L.e: The party turned out to be a great success. It turned out that she had known all along. The excitement soon died down. Don't worry – the fuss will blow over. The council laid on extra buses for the festival.

units.O: Describe a public event you attended – a concert, a match or a festival – and how it went. Use at least eight phrasal verbs from this unit.

units.sub: crop up, get out of hand, blow over

L.p: Problems *crop up* or *come up* (appear unexpectedly), and difficulties *build up* (increase gradually). Work *piles up* when you can't keep up with it. A situation *gets out of hand* when it can no longer be controlled, and things *get on top of* you when you feel unable to cope.

L.e: A few problems have cropped up with the new system. Tension had been building up for weeks. My emails piled up while I was on holiday. The party got out of hand when uninvited guests arrived. Everything is getting on top of me at the moment.

L.x: Things *got out of hand* (not *got out of hands*) when the crowd grew.

L.p: You *face up to* a difficult situation when you accept it and deal with it. You *put up with* problems you can't change, and you *come up against* opposition or difficulties (meet them). A situation can *boil down to* one simple issue, and you *get through* a hard time when you survive it.

L.e: You have to face up to the fact that you need help. The council came up against fierce opposition. In the end, it all boils down to trust. We'll get through this together.

L.p: Things *look up* when they start to improve, and they *settle down* when they become calm again. A storm or a quarrel *blows over* (passes). Business *picks up* when it gets better, and a person *bounces back* when they recover quickly after a problem.

L.e: Things are looking up – I've found a new job. Life settled down after the baby's first few months. Their row soon blew over. Sales picked up towards the end of the year. She bounced back quickly after her illness.

units.sub: find out, fill in, give away

L.p: You *find out* facts, *look up* information in a book or online and *look into* a matter (investigate it). Parents and managers *check up on* people to see whether they are behaving or working properly. Informally, you *dig up* old facts or *ferret out* hidden information (find it after a long search).

L.e: I found out where she lives. Look up the opening times online. The council is looking into the complaint. My mum still checks up on me every evening. The journalist ferreted out the truth after months of work.

L.x: Please *find out* (not *find*) what time the train leaves.

L.p: You *fill someone in* when you give them the latest details (informal), and you *pass on* information or a message to someone else. You *put out* a statement when you make it public. Information *gets out* or *leaks out* when people learn it although it was meant to be secret, and you *give away* a secret when you tell it by mistake.

L.e: Can you fill me in on what happened at the meeting? I'll pass on your message. The police put out a statement this morning. News of the takeover leaked out before the official announcement. Don't give away the ending of the film!

L.p: You *fill in* (or *fill out*) a form and *write down* or *take down* details. You *read through* a document and *go through* a list (examine it item by item). Something important *stands out* on a page, and you *mark up* or *tick off* items when you have checked them.

L.e: Please fill in your name and address in capital letters. The receptionist took down my details. I read through the contract twice. Let's go through the list together. Tick off each item as you pack it.

units.sub: sort out, work out, come up with

L.p: You *think over* a problem (consider it carefully), *talk it over* with a friend and *work out* a solution. You *figure out* how something works (informal), and you *come up with* an idea or an answer when you think of it. When you weigh possibilities, you *rule out* those that are impossible.

L.e: I need some time to think it over. Why don't you talk it over with your parents? We'll work out a solution together. I can't figure out what's wrong with the printer. She came up with a clever way to save money. The doctors have ruled out a serious infection.

L.p: You *sort out* a problem when you deal with it successfully, and you *iron out* small difficulties. You *deal with* complaints, *see to* something that needs attention and *get round* an obstacle by finding a way to avoid it. You *patch up* a quarrel when you end it, at least for a while.

L.e: The plumber sorted out the leak in ten minutes. We still need to iron out a few details. Don't worry – I'll see to the tickets. We got round the problem by hiring a van. They had a row but soon patched it up.

L.x: The plumber *sorted out* (not *solved out*) the problem in ten minutes.

L.p: Some problems *drag on* for months. A solution may *fall through* (fail) or simply not *work out*. When you have no better option, you *fall back on* something (use it as a reserve). Sometimes you just have to *put up with* a problem or *live with* it.

L.e: The dispute dragged on for over a year. The plan to rent the hall fell through. Their marriage didn't work out. If the job falls through, I can always fall back on teaching. We'll just have to live with the noise.

L.p: Before deciding, you *mull over* a question (think about it carefully for some time) and *weigh up* the options. You *opt for* one choice, or informally *plump for* it. You *decide on* something after thinking, and you *settle on* a choice after considering several. Options that are impossible are *ruled out*.

L.e: I'll mull it over and let you know tomorrow. We weighed up the pros and cons. In the end we opted for the cheaper flat. I plumped for the chocolate cake. After weeks of discussion, they settled on a name for the baby. We've ruled out going abroad this year.

L.x: We finally *decided on* (not *decided for*) the blue sofa.

L.p: You *draw up* a plan or a list (prepare it carefully) and *map out* your future (plan it in detail). You *pencil in* a meeting when you arrange it provisionally, and you *firm up* plans when you make them definite. You *count on* someone when you rely on them to help.

L.e: We drew up a list of guests. She has her whole career mapped out. Shall I pencil in Tuesday for lunch? Let's firm up the details next week. Can I count on your support?

L.p: Plans can *fall through* (fail to happen), and people *back out of* arrangements they made. You *go back on* a decision or a promise when you change it. In informal British English, you *chop and change* when you keep changing your mind. You *stick to* a plan when you don't change it, and you *go ahead with* it when you do what you planned.

L.e: Our trip to Italy fell through. He backed out of the deal at the last minute. The council has gone back on its decision. Stop chopping and changing – just choose one! Let's stick to the original plan. We're going ahead with the wedding in June.

units.sub: fall out, stand up to, back down

L.p: People *fall out* when they argue and stop being friendly. Informally, you *have it out with* someone when you discuss a problem angrily in order to settle it. You *argue over* something you disagree about, and a person who *flares up* suddenly becomes angry.

L.e: The brothers fell out over their father's will. I'm going to have it out with him tonight. They argued over who should pay. He flares up at the smallest criticism.

L.x: The two brothers *fell out* (not *fell off*) over money.

L.h: B Standing firm or giving in

L.p: You *stand up to* someone when you refuse to accept unfair treatment from them, and you *stick to your guns* when you refuse to change your opinion. You *hold out* when you continue to resist. The opposite is to *back down* (stop demanding because you can't win), *give in* (accept defeat) or *climb down* (admit you were wrong).

L.e: She stood up to the bullies in her class. Despite the criticism, he stuck to his guns. The workers held out for a better pay offer. The minister was forced to back down. After an hour of arguing, I gave in. The company has climbed down over the new charges.

L.p: After an argument, people *make up* (become friends again) or *patch things up*. You *smooth over* an awkward moment when you make it seem less serious, and you *talk* a problem *through* when you discuss it in detail.

L.e: They had a terrible row but made up the next day. We tried to patch things up for the children's sake. She smoothed over the awkward moment with a joke. Let's sit down and talk it through.

units.sub: talk into, win over, bring round

L.p: You *talk someone into* doing something when you persuade them, and you *talk someone out of* it when you persuade them not to. You *win someone over* or *bring someone round* when you persuade them to agree after they disagreed. You *push for* something when you try hard to get it, and you *press for* changes when you demand them.

L.e: She talked me into joining the choir. My friends talked me out of buying a motorbike. It took weeks, but we won the neighbours over. Dad was against the idea, but Mum brought him round. Parents are pushing for a new crossing outside the school. Campaigners are pressing for stricter laws.

L.x: He *talked me out of* (not *talked me off*) leaving my job.

L.p: You *egg someone on* when you encourage them to do something, often something silly. You *put someone up to* something when you suggest they do it, usually something wrong. Informally, you *lean on* someone when you put pressure on them, and you *push someone into* something when you force them to do it. You *go along with* an idea when you agree, perhaps unwillingly.

L.e: His friends egged him on to jump into the river. Who put you up to this? The company leaned on its suppliers to cut prices. Don't let anyone push you into a decision. I didn't like the plan, but I went along with it.

L.p: Salespeople *talk up* a product (make it sound better than it is), and politicians *play down* problems (make them seem less serious). You *come round to* an idea when you start to accept it, and you *fall for* a trick when you believe it. You *hold out for* a better offer when you refuse to accept less.

L.e: The estate agent talked up the 'cosy' kitchen. The government is playing down the risks. I didn't like the new design, but I've come round to it. Don't fall for those 'free gift' adverts. The striking workers are holding out for a better deal.

L.p: You *build someone up* when you praise them to increase their confidence or reputation, and in informal British English you *big someone up*. You *make a fuss of* someone when you give them lots of attention and affection. You *look up to* someone you admire.

L.e: The coach built up the young players before the final. The press have been bigging up the band for months. The children made a fuss of their grandmother on her birthday. Many young players look up to the captain.

L.p: You *run down* someone or something when you criticise them unfairly, and you *put someone down* when you make them feel stupid. You *pick on* someone when you treat them unfairly or bully them, and informally you *have a go at* someone when you criticise them angrily. Critics *pull apart* a film or a plan, or *pick holes in* it, when they find all its faults.

L.e: He's always running down his colleagues. Her father constantly put her down. Bigger boys used to pick on him at school. My boss had a go at me for being late. The critics pulled the play apart. The lawyer picked holes in the witness's story.

L.x: The older boys used to *pick on* (not *pick at*) him.

L.p: You *tell someone off* – or, in British English, *tick someone off* – when you speak angrily to them about something they did wrong. Schools and authorities *come down on* bad behaviour (criticise or punish it severely), and informally the press can *lay into* a public figure. You *let someone off* when you decide not to punish them.

L.e: The teacher told us off for talking. My mum ticked me off for forgetting her birthday. The school is coming down hard on bullying. The newspapers laid into the minister. The police officer let him off with a warning.

units.sub: watch out, calm down, back off

L.p: Short phrasal verbs are often used as warnings. *Watch out!* and *Look out!* warn of danger, and you can say *look out for* a particular danger. In British English, *Mind out!* means move or be careful. *Hang on!* (informal) means wait, and *Steady on!* (British English, informal) tells someone to be calmer or less extreme.

L.e: Watch out! There's a car coming! Look out for ice on the pavements. Mind out – I'm coming through with hot soup. Hang on, I'll just get my coat. Steady on – there's no need to shout.

L.x: *Watch out!* (not *Look after!*) The floor's wet.

L.p: *Calm down!* tells someone to be less angry or excited. *Pipe down!* (informal) means be quieter. *Back off!* tells someone to stop threatening or annoying you, and in informal British English *Leave off!* means stop doing something annoying. *Knock it off!* (informal) simply means stop it.

L.e: Calm down – I'm sure there's an explanation. Pipe down, children, I'm on the phone. Back off! This is none of your business. Leave off – I'm trying to concentrate! Knock it off, you two!

L.p: *Come on!* encourages someone to hurry or try harder. *Go on!* encourages someone to do something, and *Cheer up!* tells someone to be happier. *Hurry up!* asks someone to be quicker, *Keep it up!* tells them to continue doing well, and *Hang in there!* (informal) tells them not to give up.

L.e: Come on, we'll miss the bus! Go on – ask her to dance. Cheer up – you'll do better next time. Hurry up, the film's starting. Great work – keep it up! Hang in there – the exams are nearly over.

units.sub: pick up, read out, go over

L.p: A teacher *hands out* worksheets, *reads out* a list or text, and *goes over* answers with the class. In British English, students *rub out* pencil mistakes. Students put up their hands rather than *call out* answers, and they *hand in* homework when it is finished.

L.e: The teacher handed out a worksheet on the past simple. She read out the list of winners. Rub out any mistakes neatly. Let's go over the answers together. Put up your hand – don't call out! Please hand in your homework by Monday.

L.x: Please *read out* (not *read loud*) your answer to the class.

L.p: You *pick up* a language or skill when you learn it without formal study, and you *take in* information when you understand and remember it. You *brush up on* something when you improve a skill you have partly forgotten. Informally, you *catch on* when you start to understand, and you *get the hang of* something when you learn how to do it.

L.e: Children pick up languages quickly. There was too much information to take in. I need to brush up on my French before the trip. She caught on very quickly. Once you get the hang of it, it's easy.

L.h: C Falling behind and keeping up

L.p: Students who miss classes *fall behind* and have to *catch up on* the work. You *keep up with* the class when you learn at the same speed as the others. Some students *drop out* of a course before the end, and some *mess about* in class (behave in a silly way).

L.e: I fell behind after two weeks off sick. You'll need to catch up on the reading. It was hard to keep up with the others at first. Several students dropped out after the first term. Stop messing about at the back!

units.sub: sign up for, swot up, scrape through

L.p: You *sign up for* a course when you register for it, and you *put in for* a scholarship or a place when you apply for it. A university *takes in* a certain number of new students each year, and newcomers *settle in* during their first weeks. If you change subjects, you *change over* to a different one.

L.e: I've signed up for an evening course in photography. He's put in for a scholarship to study in Canada. The university takes in about two thousand students a year. Most freshers settle in within a few weeks. I changed over to chemistry in my second year.

L.x: I've *signed up for* (not *signed in for*) a pottery class.

L.p: In informal British English, students *swot up on* a subject or *mug up on* it before an exam (study it hard and quickly). They *read up on* topics (read a lot about them) and *go over* their notes. Exams always seem to *come up* faster than expected.

L.e: I need to swot up on European history this weekend. He mugged up on the dates on the bus. She read up on the company before the interview. Go over your notes the night before. The exams came up much faster than I expected.

L.p: You *sail through* an exam when you pass it easily, *scrape through* when you only just pass, and *mess up* an exam (informal) when you do it very badly. Answers with careless mistakes are *marked down*. You *get through* an exam when you pass it.

L.e: She sailed through her driving test. I only just scraped through the maths paper. I completely messed up the oral exam. Spelling mistakes will be marked down. He got through all his exams at the first attempt.

units.sub: flick through, jot down, crop up

L.p: You *flick through* or *leaf through* a book when you look at the pages quickly. You *skim through* a text to get the general idea. You *dip into* a book when you read parts of it, and you *pore over* a text when you study it carefully. Unfamiliar words *crop up* (appear) as you read.

L.e: I flicked through the magazine at the dentist's. Skim through the article first, then read it carefully. It's a book you can dip into on the train. He pored over the old maps for hours. Several new words cropped up in the text.

L.x: I *flicked through* (not *flicked on*) a magazine while I waited.

L.p: You *jot down* ideas (write them quickly), and later you *write up* your notes (write them in a complete form). A good essay *sets out* its arguments clearly and *backs up* its points with evidence. You *cut out* parts that are not needed.

L.e: Jot down any ideas that come to you. I need to write up my lab notes tonight. The essay sets out three main arguments. Back up your claims with examples. Cut out any repetition.

L.p: You *read through* your work to check it and *tidy up* the presentation. You hand in your work by the deadline (American English: *turn in*). Teachers *give back* marked work, and you *look over* their comments carefully.

L.e: Read through your essay before you hand it in. I tidied up the references at the end. Students in the US turn in their assignments online. The teacher gave back our essays this morning. Look over her comments carefully.

units.sub: take on, lay off, step down

L.h: A Getting and starting a job

L.p: Employers *take on* staff (employ them), and sports clubs *sign up* players. You *turn down* an offer you don't want. You *start out* in a career, *settle into* a new job, and *take over from* someone when you start doing the job they did before.

L.e: The supermarket is taking on fifty new staff for Christmas. The club has signed up two new players. She turned down a job in New York. He started out as a junior reporter. I'm still settling into my new job. Who will take over from you when you leave?

L.x: The firm is *taking on* (not *taking in*) new staff.

L.p: You *move up* to a higher position or *work your way up* through a company by effort. You *put in for* promotion or a transfer when you apply for it. A leader *steps down* when they leave an important job. A company *lays off* workers when there isn't enough work for them, and informally you *pack in* a job when you leave it.

L.e: She moved up quickly to become head of sales. He worked his way up from the factory floor. I've put in for a transfer to the Paris office. The chief executive stepped down after the scandal. The factory laid off two hundred workers. I'm going to pack in my job and travel.

L.p: You *clock in* when you record your arrival at work and *clock off* when you leave. You *fill in for* a colleague, or *stand in for* them, when you do their job while they are away. You *knuckle down* (informal) when you start working hard.

L.e: We have to clock in by nine. Can you fill in for me on Friday? The deputy head stood in for the head teacher. It's time to knuckle down and get some work done.

units.sub: snowed under, catch up on, knuckle down

L.p: When you have far too much work, you are *snowed under* (informal). Work *piles up* when you can't finish it, and you *take on* too much when you agree to more than you can do. You are *tied up* when you are busy and can't do anything else, and in British English you are *run off your feet* when you are extremely busy.

L.e: I'm snowed under with work this week. The paperwork piles up when I'm away. I've taken on too much and I'm exhausted. I'm tied up in meetings all morning. We've been run off our feet since the sales started.

L.x: I'm *snowed under* (not *snowed in*) with work this week.

L.p: You *get down to* work when you start it seriously, and you *press on* when you continue despite problems. You *catch up on* work you haven't done and *work through* lunch when you work without stopping. You *stay behind* when you remain at work after others have gone.

L.e: Let's get down to business. It was late, but we pressed on until we'd finished. I'm staying in this weekend to catch up on my reading. She often works through her lunch break. I stayed behind to finish the report.

L.p: When you are too busy, you *cut back on* your hours (reduce them) or take time off to *wind down* (relax gradually). Months of long days without a break can make you *burn out*, until you have no energy left at all. You can also *hand over* some of your work to colleagues.

L.e: I've cut back on my hours to four days a week. I need a holiday to wind down. She's taking a day off next week. If you don't slow down, you'll burn out. Can I hand over some of these files to you?

units.sub: pay off, save up, run up

L.p: You *bring in* money when you earn it, and you *save up* for something you want to buy. In British English you *put by* money for the future. You *live off* your salary or savings when you use them to pay for what you need, and you *scrape by* when you only just have enough.

L.e: She brings in about £2,000 a month. I'm saving up for a new bike. We put by a little every month for holidays. He lives off his savings. Students often scrape by on very little.

L.x: I'm *saving up* (not *saving on*) for a new laptop.

L.p: You *pay in* money when you put it into a bank account, and you *pay back* money you borrowed. You *pay off* a debt when you pay all of it. Informally, you *fork out* a lot of money when you pay it unwillingly, and in British English you *splash out* when you spend a lot on something special.

L.e: I paid in my wages this morning. It took us twenty years to pay off the mortgage. We had to fork out £500 for car repairs. I splashed out on a new dress for the wedding. When will you pay me back?

L.p: You *run up* a bill or debts when you let them become large, and costs *mount up* when they grow. You *fall behind with* payments when you don't pay on time. When prices *go up*, many people *cut back on* spending.

L.e: He ran up a huge phone bill while he was abroad. The interest soon mounts up. They fell behind with their rent. Prices have gone up again. We're trying to cut back on eating out.

units.sub: snap up, sell out, shop around

L.p: You *shop around* when you compare prices in different shops. You *snap up* a bargain when you buy it quickly before others do, and you *stock up on* things when you buy a lot to keep in reserve. You *pick up* something cheap when you find and buy it. Informally, you *pay up* when you pay what you owe, often unwillingly.

L.e: It's worth shopping around for car insurance. Shoppers snapped up the bargains in the January sales. We stocked up on bottled water before the storm. I picked up this jacket for £20 in a charity shop. Come on – pay up!

L.x: I *picked up* (not *took up*) a real bargain at the market.

L.p: Shops *sell out* of a product when they have none left, and a concert sells out when all the tickets have gone. A business *sells off* old stock cheaply, and in British English people *sell up* when they sell their house or business, often to retire. Shops *mark down* goods (reduce their price) in a sale.

L.e: The shop sold out of umbrellas in an hour. They're selling off last season's stock. The owners are selling up and moving to Spain. All winter coats have been marked down by 30%. Competition has brought down the price of flights.

L.p: Informally, a shop or taxi driver *rips you off* when they charge you too much, and something far too expensive is *a rip-off*. You *take back* faulty goods to the shop, and you *send back* things you ordered online. A company may give you something to *make up for* a problem.

L.e: That taxi driver ripped us off. Twenty pounds for a sandwich? What a rip-off! I took the kettle back because it didn't work. You can send back anything you don't like within 30 days. They gave us a voucher to make up for the delay.
