units.sub: take over, set up, close down

L.h: A Starting and growing a business

L.p: You *set up* a business, and a new, small company is a *start-up*. A business *takes off* when it becomes successful quickly, and it *branches out* when it starts offering new products or services. Companies *team up with* partners when they work together, and one owner *buys out* another when they buy their share.

L.e: She set up her own design business at twenty-four. He works for a tech start-up in Leeds. Sales really took off after the advert. The bakery has branched out into catering. The two firms teamed up to develop the product. He bought out his partner and now owns the whole company.

L.x: The bakery has *branched out* (not *branched off*) into catering.

L.p: A large company *takes over* a smaller one when it buys and controls it; this is a *takeover*. Firms *sell off* parts of the business they don't want and *close down* branches or factories. In hard times, some businesses *go under* – fail completely.

L.e: The supermarket chain was taken over by an American group. The takeover was worth £2 billion. The bank is selling off its insurance business. Two local branches are closing down. Many small firms went under during the crisis.

L.p: Lawyers *draw up* contracts. In meetings, people *put forward* proposals and *follow up* on decisions (take further action). You *bring forward* a meeting when you move it to an earlier time, and you *iron out* small problems before signing a deal.

L.e: Our lawyers drew up the contract. She put forward a proposal to cut costs. I'll follow up on this with the suppliers. The meeting has been brought forward to Monday. We need to iron out a few details before we sign.

units.sub: hang up, get through, call back

L.p: In British English you *ring up* someone, and you *call* them *back* when you return their call. You *get through* when you are connected, and you are *cut off* when the call ends suddenly. A receptionist *puts you through* to the right person and may ask you to *hold on* (wait).

L.e: I rang up the cinema to book tickets. Could you ask him to call me back? I've been trying to get through all morning. The train went into a tunnel and we got cut off. Hold on, I'll put you through to the accounts department.

L.x: Please *hold on* (not *hold up*) – I'll connect you.

L.p: You *hang up* when you end a call, and someone *hangs up on* you when they end the call rudely in the middle. In British English you can also *ring off*. On a bad line, a voice *breaks up* (becomes unclear), and you may ask the other person to *speak up*.

L.e: He said goodbye and hung up. She was so angry that she hung up on me. I'll ring off now – my battery's low. Sorry, you're breaking up. Could you speak up? It's a bad line.

L.p: You *get back to* someone when you reply to them later, and you *pass on* a message to someone else. You *get hold of* someone when you manage to contact them. In British English you *top up* a mobile phone when you add credit to it.

L.e: I'll get back to you with a price tomorrow. Can you pass on a message to Sarah? I've been trying to get hold of you all day. I need to top up my phone before I go.

units.sub: cheer up, calm down, get over

L.p: Something *cheers you up* when it makes you happier, and something *gets you down* when it makes you unhappy. Informally, you *perk up* when you suddenly become more cheerful or lively, and you *lighten up* when you become less serious. A person *breaks down* when they start crying and can't stop.

L.e: A long walk always cheers me up. This rainy weather is getting me down. She perked up when she heard the good news. Lighten up – it's only a game! He broke down in tears at the funeral.

L.x: A call from my friend *cheered me up* (not *cheered me on*).

L.p: You *calm down* or *cool down* when you become less angry, and informally you *blow up* when you suddenly become very angry. In British English, someone who *winds you up* annoys you deliberately. You *take it out on* someone when you treat them badly because you are upset about something else.

L.e: Calm down and tell me what happened. He blew up at me for no reason. Stop winding your sister up! When she's stressed, she takes it out on her family. Let's wait until things cool down.

L.p: You *get over* a disappointment or a loss when you recover from it, and you *pull through* a serious illness when you survive it. You *bottle up* feelings when you keep them hidden, and you *open up* when you talk about them. You *let off steam* when you release strong feelings, often by doing something active.

L.e: It took her a long time to get over the divorce. He was very ill, but he pulled through. It's not healthy to bottle up your anger. After a few weeks, he began to open up about the accident. I go running to let off steam.

units.sub: ask out, get on with, settle down

L.p: You *ask someone out* when you invite them on a date, and you *go out with* someone when you have a romantic relationship with them. You *fall for* someone when you fall in love. Two people *hit it off* (informal) when they like each other immediately. In informal British English, you *chat someone up* when you talk to them in a way that shows you are attracted to them.

L.e: He finally asked her out after six months. They've been going out for two years. She fell for him the moment she saw him. We hit it off straight away. He spent the evening chatting up the woman at the bar.

L.x: She *fell for* (not *fell on*) him at first sight.

L.p: You *get on with* or *get along with* people when you have a friendly relationship. You *stand by* the people you love in difficult times, and you *count on* friends when you rely on them to help. After an argument, you *make up* (become friends again).

L.e: I get on well with my in-laws. We've always got along with our neighbours. He stood by her when she lost her job. I know I can count on my sister. They had a row but made up quickly.

L.p: Couples *move in together* and may later *settle down* – start a quiet, stable life, often married. Informally, people *tie the knot* when they get married. Parents *bring up* children, and children *grow up* together when they spend their childhood together.

L.e: They moved in together after a year. He says he isn't ready to settle down. They tied the knot in a small church in Devon. She was brought up by her grandparents. We grew up in the same street.

units.sub: fall out, split up, make up

L.p: People *fall out with* each other when they argue and stop being friendly. Informally, you *have a go at* someone when you criticise them angrily. Someone who *picks on* you keeps criticising you unfairly, and someone who *gets at* you keeps making unkind remarks. Resentment *builds up* over time until someone explodes.

L.e: She fell out with her best friend over a boy. My brother had a go at me for borrowing his car. Why are you always picking on me? Are you getting at me? Resentment had been building up for years.

L.x: She *fell out with* (not *fell out from*) her flatmate.

L.p: Couples *split up* when their relationship ends, and one person *breaks up with* the other. A partner who leaves suddenly *walks out on* the other, and in British English you *finish with* someone when you end your relationship. People *drift apart* when they gradually become less close. After a break-up, you need time to *get over* someone.

L.e: They split up after ten years together. She broke up with him by text message. He walked out on his wife and children. She finished with him after a month. We just drifted apart after university. It took me months to get over him.

L.p: After an argument, you *make up* (become friends again) or *patch things up*. You *smooth things over* when you make a problem seem less serious, and you *talk things over* when you discuss it calmly. You *let someone off* when you decide to forgive them.

L.e: They had a terrible row but made up the next morning. We tried to patch things up for the children's sake. She sent flowers to smooth things over. Let's sit down and talk things over. I'll let you off this time.

units.sub: let on, open up, give away

L.p: You *let on* when you tell a secret, usually in the negative: *Don't let on!* You *give away* a secret when you reveal it by mistake. A secret *gets out* when people learn it. You *cover up* a mistake or a crime when you try to hide it, and you *own up* when you admit you did something wrong.

L.e: Don't let on that I told you. News of the engagement soon got out. The company tried to cover up the accident. In the end the boy owned up.

L.x: Her face *gave away* (not *gave out*) the secret.

L.p: You *open up* when you talk honestly about your feelings, and you *confide in* someone when you tell them private things. Informally, you *come out with* a remark when you say it suddenly, often surprisingly, and you *come clean* when you finally tell the truth.

L.e: After a few drinks, he started to open up. She confided in her sister about her money worries. He came out with some very strange ideas. It's time you came clean about where you were last night.

L.p: You *bring up* a subject when you mention it, and a topic *comes up* when someone mentions it. Informally, you ask *What are you getting at?* when you want to know what someone really means. You *go on about* something when you talk about it too much, and you *drift off* when you stop paying attention.

L.e: I didn't want to bring up the subject of money. Your name came up at dinner. You keep hinting – what are you getting at? He went on about his new car all evening. Sorry, I drifted off for a moment.

units.sub: grow up, bring up, pass away

L.p: Children *grow up* (become adults), and parents *bring up* their children (raise them). Children *grow out of* clothes and habits, and they often *take after* a parent – look or behave like them. In informal British English, children *play up* when they behave badly.

L.e: I grew up in a small village near the sea. She was brought up by her aunt. He's grown out of his shoes again. She takes after her father. The kids always play up when they're tired.

L.x: I *grew up* (not *grew*) in Manchester.

L.p: Young adults *move out* of their parents' home and *set up home* on their own. People *start out* with very little, and many *settle down* – start a quiet, stable life, often married. Later, they *look back on* their younger years.

L.e: She moved out when she was eighteen. They set up home in a small flat in Leeds. He travelled for years before settling down. We started out with nothing. Looking back on my twenties, I wish I'd travelled more.

L.p: People *slow down* as they get older, and some *wind down* their business before retiring. Older relatives may need someone to *look after* them. When a person dies, people often say politely that they *passed away*. Family possessions are *handed down* to the next generation.

L.e: My grandfather has slowed down a lot recently. She's winding down her business before she retires. We take turns to look after Grandma. Her husband passed away last year. This ring was handed down from my great-grandmother.

units.sub: come down with, pass out, get over

L.p: You *come down with* a cold or flu when you start to have it, and you *pick up* an infection when you catch it. Informally, you *throw up* when you are sick. You *pass out* when you become unconscious, and you *break out in* spots or a rash when they suddenly appear. If you feel tired and weak, you feel *run-down*.

L.e: Half the office is coming down with flu. She picked up a stomach bug on holiday. He threw up after the boat trip. It was so hot that two people passed out. I broke out in a rash after eating prawns. I've been feeling run-down lately.

L.x: He *passed out* (not *passed away*) in the heat but soon felt better.

L.p: A doctor *checks you over* (examines you). Informally, nurses *patch you up* when they treat your injuries quickly. You *cut out* sugar when you stop eating it completely, and you *give up* smoking. A rash or an infection *clears up* when it goes away.

L.e: The doctor checked me over and said I was fine. They patched him up and sent him home. I've cut out sugar from my diet. My dad gave up smoking ten years ago. The rash cleared up in a week.

L.p: You *get over* an illness when you recover, and you *pull through* a serious illness when you survive it. You *come round* after being unconscious. You *shake off* a cold when you get rid of it, and you *build up* your strength after an illness. When you are out of bed and active again, you are *up and about*.

L.e: It took me a week to get over the flu. He was very ill, but the doctors think he'll pull through. She came round an hour after the operation. I can't shake off this cough. Eat well to build up your strength. Grandad is up and about again after his fall.

units.sub: warm up, knock out, take up

L.p: You *take up* a sport when you start doing it. You *join in* a game with others, *sign up for* a team or a race, and *drop out* if you stop before the end. You *work out* when you exercise to get fit, often at a gym.

L.e: I took up tennis when I was twelve. Anyone can join in – no experience needed. I've signed up for a half-marathon. Three runners dropped out because of the heat. She works out at the gym every morning.

L.x: I *took up* (not *took on*) golf when I retired.

L.p: Before exercise you *warm up* with gentle movements, and afterwards you *cool down*. A football match *kicks off* when it starts. One team *takes on* another when it plays against it, and a team *falls behind* when the other side scores more.

L.e: Always warm up before you run. Remember to cool down after training. The match kicks off at three o'clock. United take on Chelsea on Saturday. We fell behind in the second half.

L.p: A team *knocks out* another team when it beats it and ends its place in a competition. A team *goes out* of a cup when it loses, and it *goes through* to the next round when it wins. A side that keeps its lead until the end *holds on* to win, and fans *cheer on* their team.

L.e: We were knocked out in the second round. England went out on penalties. They went through to the final after a late goal. Ten men held on for a famous victory. The fans cheered the team on in the pouring rain.

units.sub: tidy up, wash up, lie in

L.p: You *wake up*, *get up* (get out of bed) and, in British English, sometimes *lie in* – stay in bed later than usual. You *do up* buttons and zips. At night you may *nod off* (fall asleep without meaning to) in front of the television.

L.e: I woke up at six but didn't get up until seven. On Saturdays we lie in until ten. Do up your coat – it's cold. I nodded off in front of the TV.

L.x: I *get up* (not *stand up*) at seven every day.

L.p: You *tidy up* a room, *clear up* after a meal (remove the dishes and mess) and, in British English, *wash up* (wash the dishes). You *put away* the shopping, *hang out* the washing to dry and *throw out* things you don't need any more.

L.e: Tidy up your bedroom before your grandparents arrive. I'll clear up if you cook. It's your turn to wash up. Put the shopping away, please. I hung out the washing before it rained. We threw out loads of old magazines.

L.p: You *turn off* lights and machines when you stop them working, and you *turn down* the heating when you make it lower. You *plug in* a kettle (connect it to the electricity). You *lock up* when you lock all the doors, and you *lock yourself out* when you leave your keys inside.

L.e: Turn off the lights when you leave a room. Can you turn the heating down? It's boiling in here. Plug in the kettle, will you? Don't forget to lock up before you leave. I locked myself out and had to call a locksmith.

units.sub: go out, drop in, put up

L.p: You *go out* when you leave home for entertainment, and you *take someone out* when you take them somewhere and pay. You *meet up with* friends, *hang out* together (informal) and *eat out* (have a meal in a restaurant). A party *livens up* when it becomes more fun.

L.e: We go out most Friday nights. He took her out for dinner on her birthday. Let's meet up with Sam for coffee next week. We used to hang out at the shopping centre. We eat out about once a week. The party livened up after midnight.

L.x: We *eat out* (not *eat outside*) about once a week – usually Italian.

L.p: You *drop in* or, in British English, *pop in* when you visit someone without arranging it. You *have people round* when you invite them to your home. You *put someone up* when they sleep at your house, and a guest *stays over*. You *see someone off* when you say goodbye at a station or airport.

L.e: Drop in any time you're in the area. I'll pop in on my way home. We're having some friends round on Saturday. My cousin is putting me up while I'm in London. It's late – why don't you stay over? We went to the airport to see them off.

L.p: You *bring along* a friend when you bring them with you. People *turn up* (arrive) at a party, and the party *goes on* until late. It *breaks up* when people start to leave, and a guest who leaves quietly *slips away*.

L.e: Bring along your friends – the more the merrier. Only half the guests turned up. The party went on until three in the morning. It broke up when the neighbours complained. I slipped away before midnight.

units.sub: eat out, cut down on, polish off

L.p: You eat out at a restaurant or *eat in* at home. In informal British English you *tuck in* when you start eating with enthusiasm, and you *polish off* food when you eat all of it. You *pick at* your food when you eat only small amounts, and you *wolf down* food when you eat it very fast.

L.e: Shall we eat out tonight or eat in? Dinner's ready – tuck in! The kids polished off a whole pizza. She just picked at her salad. He wolfed down his breakfast and ran for the bus.

L.x: The children *polished off* (not *cleaned off*) the whole cake.

L.p: You *cut down on* sugar or salt when you eat less of it, and you *cut out* foods you stop eating completely. You *go off* a food when you stop liking it. You *fill up on* bread or snacks when you eat so much that you are full, and you *live on* a food when it is nearly all you eat. You *put on* weight when you get heavier, and you *work off* calories by exercising.

L.e: Since January my husband has cut down on beer. My doctor told me to cut out salt. I went off meat after watching a documentary. Don't fill up on bread before the main course. As a student, I lived on pasta. I put on three kilos over the holidays. I went for a long walk to work off lunch.

L.p: Informally, you *whip up* a meal when you make it quickly. You *heat up* leftovers and *dish up* food when you serve it. Milk *boils over* when it rises and spills out of the pan. You *top up* someone's glass when you fill it again.

L.e: I can whip up a quick omelette. Heat up the soup in the microwave. Dad dished up the Sunday roast. Watch the milk – it's boiling over! Can I top up your glass?

units.sub: clear up, cloud over, pour down

L.p: The weather *clears up* when it becomes fine after rain, *brightens up* when it becomes sunnier and *warms up* when it becomes warmer. The sun *comes out* from behind the clouds. A storm *blows over* when it passes.

L.e: It rained all morning but cleared up after lunch. The forecast says it will brighten up later. It's starting to warm up at last. The sun came out just as we reached the beach. The storm blew over during the night.

L.x: The weather *cleared up* (not *cleaned up*) in the afternoon.

L.p: The sky *clouds over* when it becomes covered with cloud. Rain *pours down*, and in informal British English it *buckets down*. The wind *picks up* when it becomes stronger, and the weather *closes in* when it gets worse and you can't see far.

L.e: It clouded over in the afternoon. The rain poured down all day. It's absolutely bucketing down out there! The wind picked up as we reached the top of the hill. The climbers turned back when the weather closed in.

L.p: Heavy snow can *cut off* villages, and lightning can *knock out* the electricity. You *wrap up* warm in cold weather and *thaw out* by a fire afterwards. You are *snowed in* when snow stops you leaving home, and in British English a match is *rained off* when rain stops it.

L.e: Heavy snow cut off several villages. The storm knocked out the electricity for hours. Wrap up warm – it's freezing. We came in and thawed out by the fire. We were snowed in for three days. The match was rained off.

units.sub: set off, check in, see off

L.p: You *set off* when you start a journey, and informally you *head off* when you leave. You *see someone off* when you say goodbye to them at a station or airport. You *drop someone off* when you take them somewhere by car and leave them there, and you *pick someone up* when you collect them.

L.e: We set off at dawn to avoid the traffic. I'd better head off – my train's at six. Mum came to see me off at the airport. My neighbour drops her twins off at school on her way to work. I'll pick you up at the airport.

L.x: Can you *drop me off* (not *drop me down*) at the corner?

L.h: B At the airport and hotel

L.p: At the airport you *check in* (show your ticket and leave your bags). Planes *take off* and *touch down* (land). You *get off* a bus, train or plane at the end of your journey. At a hotel you check in when you arrive and *check out* when you pay and leave.

L.e: We checked in two hours before the flight. We took off forty minutes late but still touched down in Rome before lunch. We got off the bus at the wrong stop. We checked out of the hotel at eleven.

L.p: You *stop off* somewhere during a long journey; a short stay of this kind is a *stopover*. Delays *hold you up*. You *get away* when you go on holiday, and you *look round* a place when you visit it and see the sights.

L.e: We stopped off in Dubai on the way to Sydney. We had a two-day stopover in Singapore. Sorry we're late – we were held up at the border. We're hoping to get away for a week in August. We spent the morning looking round the old town.

units.sub: pull over, break down, speed up

L.p: A driver *pulls out* when they move into the traffic, and a bus *pulls in* when it stops at the kerb. You *speed up* when you go faster and *slow down* when you go more slowly. You *back up* when you drive backwards, for example into a parking space.

L.e: Check your mirror before you pull out. The bus pulled in at the stop. He sped up to get through the lights. Slow down – there's a school ahead. She backed up carefully into the space.

L.x: *Slow down* (not *speed down*) – there's a school ahead.

L.p: A car *breaks down* when it stops working, and you *run out of* petrol when there is none left. A driver can *knock down* a pedestrian or *crash into* another vehicle. You *flag down* a taxi or a car when you wave to make it stop.

L.e: Our car broke down on the motorway. We ran out of petrol ten miles from home. He was knocked down on a zebra crossing. A van crashed into the back of us. We flagged down a passing taxi.

L.p: You *fill up* the tank with petrol and *pump up* the tyres. Illegally parked cars may be *towed away*. A car is *written off* when it is too damaged to repair, and you *trade in* your old car when you give it as part of the payment for a new one.

L.e: Fill up the tank before the long drive. I need to pump up the back tyres. Illegally parked cars will be towed away. The car was written off after the crash. I traded in my old car for a new hybrid.

units.sub: plug in, switch off, turn up

L.p: You *switch on* a machine to start it and switch it off to stop it. You *turn up* the volume to make it louder and *turn down* the volume to make it quieter. You *plug in* a device when you connect it to the electricity. A computer *starts up* when it begins working, and you *set up* new equipment when you get it ready to use.

L.e: Switch on the TV – the news is starting. Turn the music down, please! Plug in the charger before you go to bed. The computer takes ages to start up. It took me an hour to set up my new printer.

L.x: *Switch off* (not *close*) the TV before you go to bed.

L.p: Machines *break down*, or in informal British English they *pack up*. Batteries *run down* when they lose power. A network *goes down* when it stops working for a time, and an engine *cuts out* when it stops suddenly. You *wear out* something when you use it so much that it no longer works.

L.e: The washing machine has broken down again. My old laptop finally packed up. My phone battery ran down halfway through the call. The network went down for two hours. The engine cut out at the traffic lights. I've worn out the keys on this keyboard.

L.p: New devices *come out* (are released), and new ideas *catch on* (become popular). Old technology is *phased out* (gradually stopped). It can be hard to *keep up with* the latest developments. Companies *roll out* a new product or service when they introduce it to everyone.

L.e: The new phone comes out next month. Smart watches have really caught on. Paper tickets are being phased out. It's hard to keep up with technology. The bank is rolling out a new app.

units.sub: log in, back up, print out

L.p: You *log in* (or *log on*) when you enter your username and password, and you *log out* (or *log off*) when you finish. You *boot up* a computer when you start it, and at the end of the day you *shut* it *down* properly. You *sign up for* an online service when you create an account, and you *set up* a new account or device.

L.e: I can't log in – I've forgotten my password. Always log out on a shared computer. It takes my laptop five minutes to boot up. Shut down your computer before you go home. I've signed up for a free trial.

L.x: I can't *log in* (not *log inside*) to my account.

L.p: You *back up* files when you make copies to keep them safe, and you *print out* a document when you make a paper copy. You *key in* (or *type in*) information, *scroll down* a page and *zoom in* to see something in more detail. You *save* work regularly and *delete* files you don't need, and you *clean up* your desktop when you organise it.

L.e: Back up your work every evening. Could you print out three copies of the agenda? Key in your password and press Enter. Scroll down until you reach the comments section. Zoom in to read the small print.

L.p: A computer *freezes* or *crashes*, and a program *hangs* (stops responding). A website *goes down*, and you *shut down* and *start up* again to fix problems. Hackers *break into* (or *hack into*) systems. You *run* a virus scan to *track down* a problem, and an IT expert *sorts out* the fault.

L.e: My laptop froze, so I had to shut it down and start it up again. The bank's website went down for three hours. Hackers broke into the company's computer network. It took the IT team all day to track down the problem. A technician came and sorted out the fault.

units.sub: break out, call for, play down

L.p: Wars, fires and fighting *break out* (start suddenly), and protests *flare up* (start or become violent suddenly). A crisis can *blow up* (develop suddenly), and an issue *crops up* when it appears unexpectedly. Talks *break down* when they fail. When the excitement around a story *dies down*, the media move on.

L.e: Fighting broke out in the capital overnight. Violence flared up again after the match. A row has blown up over the new tax. Peace talks broke down after only two days. The fuss soon died down.

L.x: Fighting *broke out* (not *broke up*) in the capital overnight.

L.p: Campaigners *call for* changes (demand them publicly), and the public *speak out* against policies. Politicians *play down* problems (make them seem less serious) and *play up* successes (make them seem more important). They *back down* when they change a decision under pressure, and they *step down* when they resign.

L.e: Parents are calling for safer roads near schools. Several doctors spoke out against the plan. The minister played down the risks. The government backed down after mass protests. The party leader stepped down after the election defeat.

L.p: Journalists *dig up* information, *follow up* a story (find out more about it) and *cover* events. News *leaks out* when secret information becomes public, and a story *breaks* when it is first reported. Newspapers *pick up on* a story when they start reporting it, and they *hush up* a scandal when they keep it secret.

L.e: A reporter dug up the minister's old emails. The paper is following up the story with interviews. Details of the deal leaked out last week. The national papers soon picked up on the story. The company tried to hush up the accident.

units.sub: break in, get away, lock up

L.p: Burglars *break in* (or *break into* a building) when they enter it illegally. Thieves *make off with* things they steal, and fraudsters *rip people off* or *con people out of* money. A gang *holds up* a bank or shop (robs it with a weapon). Criminals *get away* when they escape, and they *get away with* a crime when they are not punished.

L.e: Someone broke in while we were on holiday. Thieves broke into the shop through the roof. The robbers made off with £10,000. They conned the old man out of his savings. Two men held up a petrol station last night. The burglars got away in a stolen car. He thought he'd got away with it.

L.x: The thieves *got away* (not *went away*) in a stolen car.

L.p: The police *look into* a crime (investigate it) and *track down* suspects (find them after searching). They *round up* suspects (find and arrest several) and *take in* someone for questioning. Someone may *turn in* a criminal (tell the police where they are), or a criminal may *turn themselves in*. The police *crack down on* a type of crime when they deal with it more strictly.

L.e: Detectives are looking into the robbery. Police tracked down the gang in Spain. Several suspects were rounded up in a dawn raid. Two men were taken in for questioning. His own brother turned him in. The police are cracking down on knife crime.

L.p: Criminals are *locked up* (put in prison) or *put away* (informal) for a long time. A judge may *let someone off* (not punish them) or let them off with a warning or a fine. Prisoners can be *let out* early, and some *break out* of prison (escape). People who are wrongly convicted try to *clear* their name.

L.e: He was locked up for ten years. The judge put him away for life. She was let off with a warning. He was let out after serving half his sentence. Three prisoners broke out of the jail last night.

units.sub: crack down on, take over, step down

L.p: A person or group *takes over* when they take control of a country or organisation, and the army may *seize power* in a coup. Leaders *stand for* election (British English) and are *voted in* or *voted out*. They *cling on to* power when they try hard to keep it, and they *hand over* power when they give it to someone else.

L.e: The army took over in a bloodless coup. She's standing for election for the first time. The government was voted out after twelve years. The old president clung on to power for decades. He handed over power to his deputy.

L.x: The army *took over* (not *took on*) the country in a coup.

L.p: Governments *crack down on* crime or protests when they deal with them more strictly, and they *clamp down on* activities they want to stop. Authorities *bring in* new laws (introduce them), *do away with* old rules and *lay down* the rules that everyone must follow. People who are in charge *call the shots* (informal) and *push through* changes despite opposition.

L.e: The government is cracking down on tax evasion. Police have clamped down on illegal parking. They brought in a new law on smoking in cars. The school has done away with uniforms. The contract lays down strict rules. The council pushed through the plans despite protests.

L.p: Leaders *step down* or *stand down* when they leave their job, and they can be *forced out* or *thrown out*. People *rise up* against a ruler when they rebel, and they *stand up to* authority when they resist it. A regime *falls apart* when it collapses, and a government *backs down* when it gives way to pressure.

L.e: The prime minister stepped down after the scandal. He was forced out by his own party. The people rose up against the dictator. Ordinary citizens stood up to the soldiers. The old regime fell apart within months. The government backed down over fuel taxes.

units.sub: fill out, check out, rack up

L.p: Some phrasal verbs differ between American and British English. Americans *fill out* a form where British people usually *fill in* a form. Americans *turn in* homework (British: *hand in*), *check out* a book from a library (British: *take out*) and *wait on line* or *line up* (British: *queue up*). Americans *call* someone *up*, while British people *ring* them *up*.

L.e: Please fill out this form and return it to the front desk. Students must turn in their essays by Friday. I checked out three books from the library. We lined up for an hour to get tickets. I'll call you up when I get home.

L.x: In Britain you *fill in* (not *fill up*) a form; in America you fill it out.

L.h: B American phrasal verbs used everywhere

L.p: Many American phrasal verbs are now common internationally. You *check out* a place or a website (look at it to see what it's like). You *hang out* with friends, *rack up* points, debts or wins (collect a large number), and *bulk up* (become bigger and more muscular). You *chow down* (informal) when you eat, and you *figure out* a problem when you understand it.

L.e: Check out the new café on the corner. We hung out at the mall all afternoon. The team has racked up ten wins in a row. He's been bulking up at the gym. I finally figured out how the app works.

L.p: Australian English has some phrasal verbs of its own, often informal. You *chuck a sickie* (take a day off work pretending to be ill) or *flake out* (fall asleep because you are exhausted). People *rock up* (arrive casually, often late) and *shout* someone a drink when they buy it for them. Some, like *rock up*, are now heard in Britain too.

L.e: Half the office chucked a sickie on the day of the final. After the long drive, we flaked out on the sofa. He rocked up an hour late as usual. Put your money away – I'll shout you a coffee.

units.sub: chill out, max out, dumb down

L.p: New phrasal verbs appear all the time, often in informal speech. You *chill out* (relax) or *veg out* (relax and do nothing) after a busy week. You *max out* a credit card when you use it right up to its limit. Companies *ramp up* production when they increase it quickly.

L.e: I just want to chill out this weekend. We vegged out in front of the TV all Sunday. He maxed out three credit cards in a month. Production is being ramped up to meet demand.

L.x: I *maxed out* (not *maxed up*) my credit card on holiday.

L.p: Critics complain that television is being *dumbed down* (made simpler and less intelligent to attract more viewers), and informally a report is *sexed up* when it is made to sound more exciting than the facts allow. At work, people *reach out to* clients (contact them), *loop in* colleagues (include them in an email or discussion) and *drill down* into data (examine it in detail).

L.e: Many viewers feel that the news has been dumbed down. The report was sexed up to make the threat seem greater. I'll reach out to the client tomorrow. Can you loop me in on the email? We need to drill down into these sales figures.

L.p: Online life has brought many new phrasal verbs. You *opt out of* marketing emails when you choose not to receive them, and you *scroll through* your feed on a phone. Informally, you *zone out* when you stop paying attention. People *call out* bad behaviour when they criticise it publicly, and a post or video *blows up* when it suddenly becomes very popular.

L.e: You can opt out of marketing emails at any time. I scrolled through my feed while I waited for the bus. Sorry, I zoned out for a minute. Several users called out the company for its misleading advert. Her video blew up overnight.
